## Overview

This post explores Chapter 8, ["Style Guides and
Rules"](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch08.html), from [*Software
Engineering at Google*](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book). Written by
Shaindel Schwartz and edited by Tom Manshreck, the chapter explains how shared
coding conventions help engineers maintain software as teams grow and projects
age. A style guide covers more than indentation: it establishes expectations for
naming, documentation, language features, and code organization.

The chapter distinguishes between **rules**, which engineers must follow
unless an exception is approved, and **guidance**, which recommends useful
practices while leaving room for judgment. Both help teams make decisions,
but they carry different expectations of enforcement.

## Why Teams Need Coding Rules

Rules give a team a shared vocabulary for writing and reading code. When
engineers agree on common patterns, they can spend more time understanding a
program's behavior and less time interpreting unfamiliar conventions.
Consistency also makes it easier to review changes, move between projects,
and maintain code after its original authors have left.

Useful rules begin with an engineering goal. A team might prioritize
readability, reliability, performance, or compatibility with other systems.
Its conventions should support those needs. Google's choices reflect the
challenges of maintaining a large, long-lived codebase; another organization
may need different rules to achieve sustainable development.

## Five Principles for Effective Rules

Once a team understands why it needs rules, the next question is how to choose
useful ones. [Chapter 8](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch08.html)
describes five principles that can help us make these decisions.

1. **Rules should justify their cost.** Every additional rule takes effort to
   learn, follow, and maintain. For our team, starting with a few clearly
explained rules gives everyone a manageable set of expectations.

2. **Write for the reader.** In a Python function, a name such as
   `failed_check_count` explains more than `n`. Although the longer name takes
more time to type, another contributor can understand what it represents without
tracing every assignment.

3. **Keep conventions consistent.** Before adding a function or module, we
   should check how the surrounding code is organized. For example, functions
named `load_report` and `save_report` establish a pattern that another
contributor can follow when adding related functionality.

4. **Avoid confusing or risky code.** One relevant Python example is choosing
   between `==` and `is`. The [Python
documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/expressions.html#comparisons)
explains that `==` compares values, while `is` checks object identity. When
checking whether two strings contain the same text, using `==` makes the
intended comparison explicit.

5. **Allow justified exceptions.** Performance and compatibility requirements
   can justify approved exceptions. If an external library requires a particular
callback name, we should document that requirement before changing it to match
our preferred naming convention.

## What Belongs in a Style Guide?

The chapter identifies three purposes for style guide rules: preventing
mistakes, supporting good practices, and maintaining consistency.

For a Python project, a guide could explain how to compare values correctly,
what public function docstrings should describe, and which naming conventions
contributors should follow. Each rule should include a short explanation and an
example so that a new teammate can apply it.

A useful guide should also explain what following a rule looks like in practice.
For example, requiring a docstring does not guarantee that the documentation is
helpful. A function documented as “does the calculation” still leaves readers
wondering what it calculates and what it returns. Including an example of a
clear docstring would help contributors understand the purpose of the
requirement.

## How Rules Should Change

Rules need to be reconsidered when evidence shows that they are causing
problems. At Google, engineers can propose changes, while language experts
called **style arbiters** evaluate the trade-offs and approve updates or
exceptions.

For our team, a proposed change should identify the existing rule, show a
concrete problem, and explain how the replacement would help. If a naming
convention conflicts with an external interface, for example, the proposal
should show the affected code and explain why the conflict requires an exception
or a change.

We should also record why the decision was made. Otherwise, a future contributor
might encounter the same issue and repeat the discussion without knowing its
history.

### Case Study: Python Naming Conventions

Google initially used CamelCase for Python methods because much of its Python
code supported C++ projects. As independent Python development grew, its guide
allowed snake_case while accommodating existing code and consistency within
files.

[PEP 8](https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/#function-and-variable-names)
recommends lowercase function names with underscores between words. For example,
`calculate_total` follows this convention and separates the words in the
function's name.

However, renaming an existing public function also affects the code that calls
it. Before changing function names, we should identify those callers and plan
any necessary updates. This helps us improve consistency while preserving the
behavior that users depend on.

## Guidance and Training Support the Rules

Google supports its rules with introductory guides, short tips, and training
about its development practices. These resources help engineers understand how
to apply the conventions.

This connects to our earlier post on [Knowledge Sharing in Software
Engineering](https://developerdevelopment.com/blog/se4-fall2026/), which
discusses documentation and mentoring as ways to share knowledge across a team.

For our projects, the README or contribution guide could show a common mistake,
its corrected version, and the reason for the correction. When reviewing a
teammate's work, linking to that explanation would give them a reference they
can use again.

We can apply this approach through three actions:

- **Start** documenting important project conventions with their purpose and an
example.
- **Stop** leaving recurring explanations only in private conversations; add
them to documentation that other contributors can find.
- **Continue** discussing unclear cases in pull requests and recording the
reasons behind agreed changes.

## Automating Enforcement

After documenting coding rules, a team needs a reliable way to check whether
contributions follow them. [Chapter
8](https://abseil.io/resources/swe-book/html/ch08.html) recommends automating
enforcement where possible. Automated checks can apply the same criteria across
contributions and give developers feedback before a manual review.

The team still needs to keep its checks aligned with its documented rules. If
the guide changes but the configuration stays the same, contributors may receive
warnings that no longer reflect the team's decisions.

For our class projects, this means maintaining checks that support our agreed
conventions and documenting how everyone can run them.

### Static Analysis and Error Checkers

Static analysis examines source code without executing the program being
checked. For example, Python's [ast
module](https://docs.python.org/3/library/ast.html) represents code as a tree
containing structures such as function definitions and expressions. A checker
can inspect these structures to examine names or look for docstrings.

Tools such as [Ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/linter/) provide existing
checks for Python code, including unused imports and undefined names. The
project's configuration determines which rules are enabled.

These checks give contributors feedback about specific problems, but their
results have limits. A successful lint check means that the enabled checks
detected no violations. Tests and review are still needed to investigate whether
the program behaves correctly.

### Formatters and Presubmit Checks

Formatters apply a consistent layout to code, reducing the need for reviewers to
discuss spacing and line wrapping. The [Ruff
formatter](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/formatter/) can format Python files,
while its `--check` option reports whether formatting changes are needed without
rewriting the files.

Linting and formatting serve different purposes. For example, `ruff check` runs
lint checks, while `ruff format --check` checks formatting. A project can use
both to support its conventions.

Presubmit checks bring automated verification into the process before a change
is accepted. In a GitHub workflow, [GitHub
Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/get-started/understand-github-actions)
can run checks when a pull request is opened or updated.

For our class projects, we should continue running the configured checks locally
before pushing, addressing reported problems, and reviewing automated results
before merging. We should also keep the local checks and automated workflow
aligned so that teammates receive consistent feedback.

### Where Human Judgment Still Matters

Although automated tools can enforce coding standards, they cannot evaluate
every aspect of code quality. Some decisions, such as whether code is readable,
documentation is meaningful, or a particular design is appropriate, require
human judgment. As the chapter explains, automation works best for clearly
defined rules, while developers and code reviewers handle decisions that require
context and reasoning.

## Key Takeaways

- **Consistency matters**: Shared coding conventions make code easier to
understand, maintain, and collaborate on.

- **Prioritize readability**: Code should be written for future readers, not
just the original developer.

- **Rules should have a purpose**: Every rule should provide meaningful benefits
without creating unnecessary restrictions.

- **Automate when possible**: Tools can enforce coding standards consistently
and reduce repetitive manual checks.

- **Allow flexibility**: Coding standards should evolve over time, and some
decisions still require human judgment.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" title="Open-Source Tool for Software Engineers" collapse="false"}

Our team built `Style Guide Checker`, a lightweight Python command-line tool
that checks Python files against a set of team coding conventions.

The tool checks whether function names and filenames follow `snake_case`
conventions and whether public functions include docstrings. When a violation
is found, it provides an explanation of the issue and why following the
convention matters.

Using Python's built-in `ast` and `pathlib` modules, our project demonstrates
how automated checks can improve code readability, consistency, and
maintainability across a team.
You can view the project here: [style-guide-checker on
GitHub](https://github.com/Abishek-D-7/style-guide-checker).

:::
